answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Consequential methods may better reflect how electricity-sector actions actually change the system, capturing investment/retirement responses, technology substitution, and time- and location-specific operational effects, which EPRI has shown may matter for rooftop solar (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y), energy storage (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902), and end-use electrification (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9). Used appropriately, consequential accounting may improve decision usefulness, avoid double-counting, and clarify co-pollutant/air-quality co-benefits alongside GHGs.

Key challenges include, but may not be limited to:
• Temporal volatility and evolution: Short-run marginal signals are instantaneous and may diverge from both short-run and long-run mix a multi-decade project will face.
• Spatial heterogeneity: Margins differ across nodes and balancing areas, as EPRI work shows (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420). Using coarse regional averages may potentially mis-rank options, while overly granular inputs can reduce comparability.
• Mechanism mismatch: Operating margin approaches may omit structural change when actions scale, biasing results, as discussed in earlier EPRI work. (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119).
• Data and cost: Hourly, locational inputs and transparent documentation of counterfactuals may raise the analysis burden but are often necessary where material.
• Methods: There are a variety of approaches that have been explored to estimate locational marginal emission rates, but they all suffer from methodological and empirical problems that may render them unusable for conducting marginal electric sector impact analysis. (EPRI 2024; 3002030179; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179).

Unintended consequences for consideration:
• Perverse siting signals if instantaneous snapshots are treated as long-run project factors (EPRI 2025; 3002031420).
• Potential “over-crediting” of estimated abatement when substitution or policy constraints mean a project is infra-marginal (https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2025/program/paper/NEDSnTBF).
• Loss of comparability if methods mix operating margin snapshots with build margin effects without disclosure or sensitivities.

answers.label: Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The formula incorporates the use of marginal emissions rates, which may be inappropriate to apply to electricity procurement actions that are not marginal. By definition, a marginal rate is the change in system emissions for an increase or decrease of 1 MWh of demand or supply. Any procurement action that is more than “incremental” to the system will not correctly be quantified using a marginal rate (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420).

EPRI modeling indicates that consequential emissions estimates may be: 1. Influenced by investment and dispatch feedbacks; 2. Better informed by using power system models or long-run marginal emission rates where structural change is material. Studies that link capacity planning/dispatch to interventions like electrification, rooftop solar, and energy storage adoption show that simplified short-run marginal factors miss structural substitutions and misstate system responses.

Links to studies: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
In addition to short-run dispatch effects, consequential estimates may be more effective when considering (where material):
• Investment and retirement responses: EPRI research suggests that these structural responses can dominate consequential emissions impacts, which makes power system models or long-run marginal emission rates better-suited to capture these effects (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902).
• Technology interactions in the power sector: Representing substitution across resources and temporal correlations can alter impacts (e.g., rooftop solar displacing utility-scale solar, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).
• Cross-sector feedbacks: EPRI research indicates that integrated energy system modeling may be important for quantifying consequential impacts in areas like end-use electrification (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9) and electrolytic hydrogen production (https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002028407).
• Co-pollutant emissions and air quality effects: Changes in generator operations, entry, and exit as well as upstream/downstream emissions sources can alter non-CO2 pollutants (NOx/SO2/PM), which has air quality impacts (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9).
For each category, the research above indicates the importance of materiality-based inclusion (i.e., based on context-specific factors), transparent disclosure of methods, and sensitivity analysis to key drivers (e.g., policy, fuel prices, technology costs).

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
In theory, for interventions that plausibly change the capacity mix or system operations over time, EPRI research indicates that forward-looking consequential methods may alter assessed emissions impacts. Evidence from EPRI studies show that:
• Investment/retirement responses dominate emissions outcomes for energy storage: Dispatch-only, year-by-year snapshots may mislead; evaluating impacts across the asset’s lifetime better reflects potential consequential impacts (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902).
• Simplified short-run rates can underestimate electrification’s benefits due to grid decarbonization over time, which electrification facilitates: This dynamic may make lifetime, scenario-consistent accounting more accurate than single-year snapshots (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9).
• Rooftop PV impacts depend on substitution with grid additions over time and evolving hourly margins: Lifetime modeling (or long-run rates) may better capture these dynamics compared with annual fixed rates (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).

However, in practice, this research suggests that calculating the emissions impact over the expected lifetime of the proposed project may raise implementation challenges. Because marginal rates are constantly changing and can be expected to change with structural changes to the electricity system (e.g., new loads, changes in generation supplies), using a fixed marginal emissions rate that is estimated at the time a proposed project is being evaluated can negatively impact decision making. In addition, approaches that account for structural changes (e.g., capacity expansion modeling, long-run marginal rates) entail uncertainty at the project’s outset, which may suggest reasons for limiting analysis to the reporting year only.

answers.label: Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Additionality is a component of GHG offset programs that ensures that offset projects are not granted tradable carbon credits for non-additional actions. In general, there is no analytic method that can be used to definitively “prove” the additionality of a proposed offset project (EPRI 2011; 1023122; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000000001023122).

However, the use of additionality tests may not needed to evaluate the potential GHG emissions impact of proposed grid-connected electricity projects, unless these projects are envisioned to be eligible to receive carbon credits. Any new investments in new electricity infrastructure or changes in electricity demand may be expected to impact system-wide GHG emissions, so it may be sensible to develop methods to estimate the GHG emissions impact of new grid-connected projects regardless of whether they are additional.

The CDM and other offset programs have determined additionality using a case-by-case approach for each project (i.e., a “project-based” approach), involving the use of multiple additionality tests. Standardized approaches credit reductions on the basis of uniformly applicable criteria. These include performance standards (e.g., emission rates, energy use rates, market penetration rates) and technology benchmarks (e.g., specific technologies in certain sectors and locations that are automatically deemed additional) (EPRI 2011).
A standardized approach to baseline setting can incorporate default assumptions (e.g., BAU emissions factors) established by the regulator, thereby streamlining the baseline calculation process and reducing the amount of project-specific data required to calculate the baseline. In contrast, RGGI’s offset system requires the calculation of project-specific baselines and provides methodologies for doing so. This approach is similar to the one used by the CDM. It may be the case, however, that even under a standardized baseline approach, some project categories will require a significant amount of project-specific data and assessment (EPRI 2011).

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
EPRI has been engaged in developing approved carbon offset protocols related to reducing nitrogen fertilizer applications in agricultural crop production (EPRI 2013; 1023669; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000000001023669). This research indicates the difficulties in implementing a financial analysis test, particularly when a proposed project such as reduced nitrogen use may actually be profitable for farmers that engage in this activity. This EPRI research also suggests that farmers tend to continue to fertilize their lands beyond the economic optimum level because of “common practice.” This research suggests that it does not seem feasible in all instances to use a financial analysis test.

The EPRI research referenced above suggests that the “Common Practice” test may be used effectively to assess the additionality of certain types of offset and GHG abatement projects. In the MSU-EPRI Methodology (ACR and VCS versions), the performance test is passed at a project site if the N fertilizer rate is below a threshold that represents the business-as-usual (BAU) rate. This BAU rate is based on the yield-goal approach (historical and current common practice), and is identical to the calculated baseline N rate of the project, using either Approach 1 or 2. In the CAR NMPP, the performance standard for a project activity is based on a N use efficiency (NUE) metric termed the ratio of Removed to Applied Nitrogen (RTA) calculated as a ratio of the amount of N removed by crop biomass to the amount of N available to the crop as a function of how much total N was applied to the crop. production (EPRI 2013).

When using the ACR and VCS versions of the MSU-EPRI Methodology, project proponents must pass a Practice-Based Performance Standard Test. This standard equates the BAU baseline scenario for N fertilizer application with the common practice of producers to apply N fertilizer rates based upon recommendations derived from yield goal estimates. Project developers pass the Performance Standard Test by reducing their N fertilizer rate below the BAU rate, which is also the baseline value for N fertilizer rate for the proposed project. Reducing the N fertilizer rate (and therefore N2O emissions) below the BAU rate (Approach 1 or 2) results in project additionality. Brief evidence for the wide-scale historic and continued use of the yield-goal approach in U.S. crop agriculture, and therefore its legitimacy as a Performance Standard for testing additionality is provided un the original EPRI published report. More information can be found in Annex E of the VCS version of the MSU-EPRI Methodology (EPRI 2013).

One major reason the EPRI-MSU team proposed a Performance Benchmark was to create a site specific (project-scale) test for additionality that could act as a sectoral baseline for agricultural crop N management projects in the U.S. The research expected this approach to reduce the current need to conduct costly and time-consuming site-specific evaluations of additionality for each proposed emissions reduction project. Project developers pass the Performance Benchmark by being below a threshold value that represents a BAU application of N fertilizer – identical to the baseline N application rate at a project field. Reductions in rate, and therefore N2O emissions, below the BAU value result in project additionality. In other words, the additionality benchmark is identical in value to the crediting benchmark (EPRI 2013).

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text:
EPRI research shows emissions impacts and additionality may vary by region owing to differences in resource mix, policies, infrastructure, and other factors:
• Policy and market context: EPRI research illustrates how electricity generation resource additions are inframarginal in U.S. states that have binding emission performance standards, which implies that these “new” generation projects would otherwise have been built due to state policies (https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2025/program/paper/NEDSnTBF). EPRI analysis also illustrates regional differences in power sector planning and relative cost-effectiveness of different resources, which alters project additionality (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435124004239).
• Technology substitution varies by region: EPRI research indicates that impacts of energy storage may be region-dependent and may raise or lower emissions depending on the regional fleet, prices, and policy (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902). Rooftop solar often substitutes for utility-scale solar in high-solar regions; consequential emissions impacts differ across regions (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).
• Financial viability and local practices: Additionality may be region specific in that what may be additional in one region may not be additional in another region. For example, it may be common practice for farmers to over-fertilize corn grown in the Upper Midwest of the United States, but this may not be common practice in other regions of the U.S. or in other parts of the world. A good example of the need for different regional approaches to determining additionality are GHG emissions offset projects designed to destroy methane (CH4) emitted from landfills. In this case, the California Air Resources Board (CARB) does not recognize landfill gas offsets implemented anywhere in the United States as being “additional,” because under existing laws and regulations in California, operators of landfills are required to capture and destroy methane emissions from landfills. However, a number of landfill gas offset projects have been successfully implemented in other U.S. states and Canada that have been granted tradable carbon offsets because these activities were deemed to be additional as these activities are not required to be done by law or regulation in these jurisdictions (EPRI 2022; 3002025723; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002025723).

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
EPRI research indicates that “appropriate” approaches match the mechanism and scale. Operating margin (OM) approaches that hold the fleet fixed (short-run dispatch response) are most appropriate for small, transitory operational changes that do not induce new builds/retirements (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119). Several ISOs/RTOs publish locational marginal emissions rates (LMERs) that can inform these operational questions (EPRI 2025, 3002031420, https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420). When projects plausibly affect the capacity mix (e.g., large-scale rooftop solar deployment, energy storage, widespread electrification), operating-margin-only methods can misstate impacts by omitting structural change, especially since the build margin can influence the operating margin, as shown in EPRI research on energy storage (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902).

Practical considerations limit OM/LMER use as standalone factors for long-lived projects:
• Temporal variability and evolution: OM/LMER signals are instantaneous and constantly changing with dispatch, congestion, and policy/fleet evolution. A factor observed today may not represent the margins faced over a multi-decade project horizon (EPRI 2024; 3002030179: https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179)
• Spatial heterogeneity and multiple marginal units: In large systems (e.g., PJM/MISO), there is nearly always congestion somewhere, so multiple resources share the margin with location-specific shift factors. This produces highly variable and sometimes large marginal rates across nodes and five-minute intervals (EPRI 2024; 3002030179: https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179).
• Forecasting limits: Because dispatch can flip between intervals (e.g., wind on the margin in one period and coal on the margin the next), OM snapshots describe what happened, not necessarily what will happen. They are ideally treated as operational indicators, not long-run project factors.

Comments on specific methods:
• A difference-based approach can be highly granular but reportedly is subject to bias since changing grid conditions confound the effect of varying load. Also, this approach may lead to extreme values based on coincidence, especially in situations where load is changing more slowly (EPRI 2024; 3002030179; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179).
• One challenge with using binning-based regression models is that using multiple bins of historical data for each hour may result in regression analyses producing different rates for different grid conditions. These models also can be inaccurate if grid conditions within a bin are not similar along a confounding dimension. The most common confounding bias is in marginal renewables (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).
• Using a heat-rate modeling approach, one may calculate a resulting MER. This approach may be both highly granular but also highly variable. EPRI research suggests that these models may perform best in power grids where there is a clearly defined fuel type on the margin (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).
• Experiment-based models reportedly can have low bias, but implementing this approach requires access and manipulation of very large, high-quality datasets. In general, EPRI research indicates that this approach may have low statistical power, and it may be difficult to produce a wide range of treatment effects under various grid conditions (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).
• One advantage of developing MER estimates based on the actual emissions of marginal generation unit is that grid operators may have access to data about the grid that is not readily available to the public, but MER estimates developed this way can be highly variable and highly granular (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text: Build margin factors may be most useful when they reflect the mix of new capacity economically induced or displaced by an action, which can be technology- and region-specific. EPRI modeling shows displacement weights vary and may not be well represented by fixed global heuristics. For instance, for rooftop solar, build margins can dominate because it frequently substitutes for utility-scale additions in many regions (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text:
Several factors can be considered when evaluating model applicability for different projects:
• Mechanism: If a project plausibly influences investment/retirement decisions (structural), due to its persistence and policy context, approaches that capture long-run system response may be more appropriate, including capacity expansion models or long-run marginal rates (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119). EPRI research indicates that energy storage (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902) and rooftop solar (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y) are technologies where emissions impacts can be dominated by investment effects rather than dispatch alone.
• Penetration level and system feedbacks: As penetration rises, projects may alter prices, curtailment, future builds, and displaced resources, especially given correlations in output across installed capacity (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301421521002949). For rooftop solar, including these dynamics reduces implied benefits by 41-98% in a U.S. case study, relative to short-run rates (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: Marginal emissions factors may differ at different geographic locations on the power grid. Given this, EPRI research indicates the importance of using locational marginal emission rates, where material, instead of marginal rates related to larger geographies (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420).

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: “Appropriate” temporal resolution likely varies based on the application, but EPRI research suggests that, where output/load co-varies hourly with marginal emissions (e.g., solar profiles, EV charging), operating margin estimates are most accurate/useful when they are at least hourly and region-specific (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902). EPRI research suggests that annualized emissions rates can over-/under-estimate effects and mis-rank options (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y). ISO locational marginal emissions rate data illustrate substantial intra-hour volatility, which reinforces the need for higher temporal resolution treatments for some applications (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420). However, data availability may limit temporal granularity based on the time interval of dispatch.

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text:
EPRI research suggests several considerations for selection:
• Endogenous/model-based weighting may be appropriate when projects can change the capacity mix. EPRI modeling shows investment (build margin) effects may dominate dispatch (operating margin) effects for technologies like battery storage, where evaluating investment and dispatch simultaneously changes the sign and magnitudes across technologies and regions (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902). This finding supports approaches that derive weights from capacity expansion modeling or long-run marginal methods for specific technologies, geographies, and scenarios rather than fixed splits.
• Weights may be most useful when they reflect technology-specific substitution. EPRI’s detailed systems modeling suggests that rooftop solar often displaces utility-scale solar rather than fossil, yielding 41% lower benefits in 2035 and 98% in 2050 versus simplified a “combined margin” approach that places 0.75 weight on the operating margin (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).
• Program design and incentives may shift build versus operating contributions for electricity-consuming projects. For EPRI analysis of hydrogen tax credits, the stringency of temporal matching, additionality, and deliverability changes power sector buildout and dispatch, which alters the relative importance of build margin and operating margin channels (https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002028407).
